title: The Impact of Strong Interpersonal Connections in the Workplace
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Citing a Gallup finding that workplace friendships are linked to dramatically higher engagement, this article surveys the research connecting close colleague relationships to satisfaction, resilience, innovation, and productivity. It describes deliberate tactics leaders use to seed these connections, informal social events, cross-functional pairing, mentorship programs, and shared-interest groups, rather than assuming friendship will form organically. The piece adds a specific, less obvious tactic: sponsoring two or three colleagues to attend an external development program together rather than sending one person alone, since shared external experiences tend to forge closer bonds.
points: A cited Gallup finding links workplace friendships to being seven times more likely to be highly engaged.
Deliberate tactics named include informal social events, cross-functional pairing, and mentorship programs.
A specific tactic: sending two or three colleagues together to an external program rather than one person alone.
Shared travel and external experiences are said to build camaraderie through a shared sense of identity.
quotes: According to a recent Gallup study, team members who have friends in the workplace are seven times more likely to be highly engaged at their jobs.
Good leaders don’t presume close working relationships will always happen organically.
Rather than sponsor a solitary team member to engage in a professional development program or experience outside of the organization, they underwrite team members to attend as dyads or triads.
When team members travel, dine, and attend sessions together over an extended period of time, they often form closer ties.
Good leaders want close relationships between colleagues to form naturally, but know sometimes they need a little push.
